title: Lectio divina, 1: read
hookLine: the monks' ladder of four steps; first, read a short passage slowly
last: I LOOK AT HIM, HE LOOKS AT ME.

lines: GUIGO, AT WORK WITH HIS HANDS.
cards: One day a Carthusian monk named Guigo was busy with work for his hands, and he started thinking about the inner work monks do. All at once, he says, four steps came to mind.

He wrote them down in a short letter to a brother monk named Gervase, and pictured them as a ladder: its foot on the ground, its top piercing the clouds. The first rung is the simplest: read. But slowly.
Not the way a thumb skims a screen, half a headline on the way to the next thing. Slowly enough to taste the words.

teach.b: First, the name. Lectio divina is Latin for divine reading, or holy reading. Monks practiced it long before Guigo: Saint Benedict's Rule sets aside hours of the day for holy reading.
Guigo's gift was to describe its steps. Second, the ladder. Four rungs: reading, meditation, prayer, contemplation, one a day for four days.
He sums them up, roughly: reading seeks, meditation finds, prayer asks, contemplation tastes.
It echoes Jesus in the Douay-Rheims: "Ask, and it shall be given you: seek, and you shall find: knock, and it shall be opened to you." Third, what reading means here. Not a lot.

A little, slowly, more than once: a single verse, a few lines at most. Benedict's Rule even asks anyone reading in the rest hour not to disturb the others, a hint that reading made a sound. Mouth and ears joined the eyes.
Guigo compares it to putting food in your mouth: you're not eating yet, but you've taken a bite.
Some take the day's Gospel from Mass, or a psalm.

teach.h: ONE VERSE FOR ALL FOUR RUNGS.
teach.b: One verse rides up all four rungs here, so you can climb with it: Jesus in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, "Come to me, all you that labour, and are burdened, and I will refresh you."

teach.h: COME TO ME, ALL YOU THAT ARE BURDENED.
teach.b: That's the whole reading. Reading slowly is the opposite of scrolling: you're not looking for the next thing. You're staying with this one.

how: Catholics practice lectio divina with the day's Mass readings, alone or in parish groups, reading a short passage slowly several times before moving on to meditation, prayer and quiet.

o: slow, prayerful reading of a short Scripture passage
studying the Bible chapter by chapter in a group
the priest's reading of the Gospel at Mass

games.q: climb the ladder — tap the pairs.
p: the Carthusian who named the four rungs

s: lectio divina means reading as much Scripture as you can
it means reading a little, slowly, more than once.
Benedict's Rule asks readers in the rest hour not to disturb the others
a hint that reading made a sound: mouth and ears, not only eyes.
monks practiced it for centuries before; Benedict's Rule sets hours for it. Guigo described its steps.

games.q: you have ten minutes to pray with Scripture. how does the first rung of lectio divina say to use them?
o: read as many chapters as you can.
read one short passage slowly, more than once.
skip the reading and just talk to God.
games.why: reading comes first, and it's slow: a verse or a few lines, repeated. Guigo compares it to taking a bite of food.

practice: Say the verse quietly, under your breath: come to me, all you that labor, and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Say it again, slower, then a third time, and notice which word catches; don't explain it yet, that's tomorrow.
Whether you pray or not, reading slowly is the whole job today.

wordCard.voice: Lectio divina. Latin for holy reading: a short passage, read slowly, the first rung of the monks' ladder. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: holy reading, the monks' slow way of reading Scripture.

carryVoice: Your line: read slowly. It's the first rung of four. Day two hundred thirty-three, done.
